_metadata.validation_note: This file was generated by AI based on publicly available New York statutes and must be reviewed by a licensed New York tenant attorney before use in any deployment advising real people. New York landlord-tenant law is complex and varies significantly by locality — NYC in particular has substantial additional protections.
primary_statutes: New York Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law (RPAPL) §711 — Grounds for summary proceeding
New York Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law (RPAPL) §735 — Service of notice
New York Real Property Law (RPL) §232-a — Month-to-month termination (NYC)
New York Real Property Law (RPL) §232-b — Month-to-month termination (outside NYC)
Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (HSTPA) — Extended nonpayment notice to 14 days
Good Cause Eviction Law (2024) — Statewide just cause protection
_metadata.portability_note: This file is the NY-specific rules layer. Swap for ca_eviction_rules.json or tx_eviction_rules.json to apply the same reasoning engine to California or Texas.
key_differences_from_ca_and_tx: Nonpayment notice: 14 days (much longer than CA/TX's 3 days — extended by HSTPA 2019)
Statewide Good Cause Eviction Law (2024) — comparable in scope to CA's AB 1482
NYC has its own rent stabilization and rent control systems with substantial additional protections
Notice periods for termination graduate by tenancy length: <1 year = 30 days; 1-2 years = 60 days; 2+ years = 90 days
RPAPL §735 service requirements are specific and strictly construed — improper service is a common defense

nonpayment_of_rent.notes: CRITICAL DIFFERENCE FROM CA/TX: New York requires 14 days for a nonpayment demand — not 3 days. This was extended from 3 days by the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019. The demand must be in writing and state the amount of rent owed.

defect_triggers.description: Notice gives fewer than 14 days to pay or vacate
defect_triggers.rule: New York requires a minimum 14-day written rent demand before an eviction proceeding may be commenced for nonpayment. A notice giving 3 days (or any period less than 14 days) is defective.

defect_triggers.description: Rent demand overstates the amount owed or includes improper charges
defect_triggers.rule: The rent demand must accurately state the amount of rent owed. Including improper charges or overstating the amount can render the demand defective.

curable_lease_violation.statute: RPAPL §753(4) (rent stabilized units); lease terms for non-stabilized
curable_lease_violation.notes: For curable lease violations, a 10-day notice to cure is standard. If tenant does not cure, landlord must then serve a Termination Notice before commencing proceedings.

defect_triggers.description: Landlord commenced eviction without serving a cure notice first
defect_triggers.rule: For curable lease violations, a notice to cure must be served before a termination notice. Skipping this step is a procedural defect.

termination_short_tenancy.notes: Outside NYC, 30-day notice required for month-to-month tenancies under 1 year. Good Cause Eviction Law (2024) may also require a stated reason.

defect_triggers.description: 30-day notice used for tenant with 1+ year tenancy (should be 60 days)
defect_triggers.rule: Tenants who have occupied a unit for 1 year or more are entitled to at least 60 days notice. A 30-day notice is insufficient.

termination_long_tenancy.notes: New York's graduated notice periods (30/60/90 days by tenancy length) are more gradated than California's two-tier system (30/60). The longer the tenancy, the more notice required.

methods.description: Delivering the notice to the tenant personally
Delivering to a person of suitable age and discretion at the premises AND mailing a copy to the tenant
Affixing to a conspicuous part of the door AND mailing a copy
methods.condition: If no person of suitable age found

defect_triggers.description: Improper service — mailing step omitted from substituted or nail-and-mail service
defect_triggers.rule: Under RPAPL §735, both steps must be completed for substituted service or nail-and-mail service. Omitting the mailing renders service defective.

defect_triggers.description: Notice period calculated incorrectly after nail-and-mail service
defect_triggers.rule: When using nail-and-mail service, an additional 5 days must be added to the notice period. Courts strictly construe this requirement.

good_cause_eviction_2024.statute: New York Good Cause Eviction Law (L. 2024, Ch. 56, Part BB)
good_cause_eviction_2024.coverage_note: New York enacted a statewide Good Cause Eviction Law in 2024. Coverage is complex — many exemptions apply. NYC was already covered by rent stabilization with stronger protections.
exemptions: Buildings with fewer than 10 units (small landlord exemption)
Owner-occupied buildings with 10 or fewer units (owner lives on premises)
Units occupied for fewer than 12 months
Housing built within the last 30 years (rolling exemption — longest exemption in US as of 2024)
Units subject to rent stabilization or rent control (covered by those systems instead)
good_cause_reasons: Nonpayment of rent (limited to rent increases that do not exceed 5% or CPI, whichever is lower)
Material violation of lease after opportunity to cure
Refusal to allow access after proper notice
Owner or immediate family member moving in (owner occupancy)

rent_increase_protection.description: A key feature of NY's Good Cause Eviction Law: eviction for nonpayment tied to a rent increase exceeding the lesser of 5% or CPI is NOT considered 'good cause.' This addresses 'eviction by rent increase.'
rent_increase_protection.note: IMPORTANT: This is a 2024 innovation not present in CA's AB 1482. If the landlord raised rent beyond the threshold and tenant couldn't pay the increase, this may be a defense.

defect_triggers.description: Good Cause covered unit: no reason stated for termination
defect_triggers.rule: For covered tenants (12+ months, non-exempt unit), any termination notice must state a qualifying good cause reason.
defect_triggers.confidence: HIGH — confirm exemption status with NY attorney

defect_triggers.description: Nonpayment tied to rent increase exceeding Good Cause threshold
defect_triggers.rule: If the tenant's nonpayment is caused by a rent increase that exceeds the lesser of 5% or CPI, the landlord may not have good cause to evict.

nyc_specific.note: New York City has its own rent stabilization and rent control systems that provide significantly stronger protections than state law. If the unit is in NYC, the following additional analysis is required.

rent_stabilization.applies_to: Most pre-1974 buildings with 6+ units in NYC; also newer buildings with government subsidies in some cases
key_protections: Landlord may only increase rent by amounts set by NYC Rent Guidelines Board (RGB)
Tenant has right to lease renewal on same terms
Landlord may only refuse renewal for limited good cause reasons
Preferential rent protections (HSTPA 2019): landlord may not raise rent above the legal regulated rent even if tenant was previously paying below it

defect_triggers.description: Rent-stabilized unit: nonpayment notice based on rent increase above RGB allowance
defect_triggers.rule: In a rent-stabilized unit, rent may only be increased by amounts set by the NYC Rent Guidelines Board. A notice demanding rent in excess of the legal regulated rent is defective.

affirmative_defenses.name: Warranty of Habitability
affirmative_defenses.description: Landlord failed to maintain the unit in habitable condition. Tenant may be entitled to a rent reduction (abatement).
affirmative_defenses.strength: STRONG if documented — NY courts take habitability seriously
affirmative_defenses.notes: In NY, a habitability breach can result in a monetary abatement (reduction of rent owed) in a nonpayment proceeding, potentially eliminating the basis for eviction.

affirmative_defenses.name: Retaliation
affirmative_defenses.description: Eviction is in retaliation for tenant exercising a legal right.
affirmative_defenses.presumption: Retaliation presumed if eviction occurs within 60 days of tenant exercising protected right (shorter presumption window than CA's 180 days)

affirmative_defenses.name: Discrimination
statutes: NYC Human Rights Law (broader than state)
affirmative_defenses.nyc_note: NYC Human Rights Law is among the strongest anti-discrimination laws in the US — additional protected classes include source of income (Section 8), lawful occupation, and others.

affirmative_defenses.name: Good Cause Eviction (Rent Increase Defense)
affirmative_defenses.description: Tenant's nonpayment resulted from a rent increase exceeding the Good Cause threshold (5% or CPI, whichever is lower).
affirmative_defenses.notes: This defense is unique to New York. If the landlord raised rent above the threshold and the tenant could not pay the increase, the landlord may lack good cause to evict. Confirm coverage and exemption status.

notice_analysis: What type of notice was served? (14-day rent demand / cure notice / termination notice)
How many days does the notice give the tenant?
What is the exact dollar amount demanded?
How long has the tenant continuously lived in the unit?
What city is the unit in? (NYC vs. other)
How many units are in the building? (affects Good Cause Eviction coverage)
Does the landlord live in the building?
When was the building built? (30-year exemption from Good Cause Eviction)
Is the unit rent-stabilized or rent-controlled? (check DHCR registration)
Did the landlord recently raise the rent? By how much?
How was the notice served? (personal / substituted / nail and mail)
If nail and mail: was the notice also mailed?
Has the tenant made any written repair requests or complained to code enforcement in the past 60 days?
